lesson.title: Gefühle: die Liebe, nett, wütend, stolz, die Freude
lesson.subtitle: love you already own, nice you already bought — and the proud ones with no twin

hook.title: Love, Neat Gone Warm, and the Two With No Twin
hook.content: die Liebe is the twin you already own: love and Liebe are the same ancient root — Proto-Germanic *leub-, 'to hold dear' — with English turning the b-sound to v (give/geben, live/leben, love/Liebe). The family is bigger than it looks: archaic English lief, 'dear', is the same word, and English believe and German glauben are the same root with the same prefix pattern — one prefix slot filled on each side, be- in English, ge- in German — all built on the root of love. nett is the double purchase: French net, 'clean, pure', from Latin nitidus, 'shining' — English bought it as neat and kept it tidy; German bought it as nett and warmed it into 'nice'. Same French word, two temperatures. die Freude is the joy of froh, 'glad' — and English frolic is the same word through Dutch vrolijk, 'merry'. wütend is die Wut, rage, wearing the adjective ending — Old English had the same word, wōd 'furious', which survives in archaic English wood, 'mad'; the dictionaries record it even though everyday English forgot it. And stolz is the honest limitation: no safe English twin exists — English proud came from Old French prud, 'valiant', a completely different family. When English needed 'proud', it bought French.

footnotes.title: The b/v Ledger
footnotes.content: The love/Liebe correspondence is one of German's steadiest: give/geben, live/leben, grave/Grab — English writes v or f where German writes b. And the ledger has a verb entry too: glauben and believe are the same old compound, ge- + the love-root on one side, be- + the love-root on the other.

pattern.title: Saying How You Feel
pattern.content: 1. The adjective stands after sein with no ending: Ich bin stolz, Du bist wütend, Er ist nett. 2. The fixed prepositions: stolz auf + accusative — Ich bin stolz auf das Haus; wütend auf — Er ist wütend auf seinen Bruder. 3. Fear takes vor + dative: Ich habe Angst vor dem Arzt — German's 'afraid of' says 'afraid before'. 4. Joy takes mit: Die Gruppe tanzt mit Freude. 5. The noun hides inside the adjective: stolz ↔ der Stolz — German builds the noun with zero change where English reshapes proud into pride.
pattern.linguist_note: nett and neat are what linguists call doublets: one French word, two languages, two divergent meanings. English neat stayed close to the Latin 'shining, clean'; German nett drifted through 'precise' into 'pleasant' — helped, some dictionaries say, by English nice, which itself wandered all the way from Latin nescius, 'ignorant'. Words wander: the tidy one became the kind one.

exercises.prompt: The feelings, named — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.german: Die Liebe ist süß wie Honig

matching_pairs.english: I am afraid of the doctor
matching_pairs.german: Ich habe Angst vor dem Arzt

matching_pairs.english: The engineer is proud of the house
matching_pairs.german: Der Ingenieur ist stolz auf das Haus

matching_pairs.english: The party makes joy, the joy of riding
matching_pairs.german: Die Party macht Freude, die Freude am Reiten

matching_pairs.english: Chess and guitar in the free time
matching_pairs.german: Schach und Gitarre in der Freizeit

exercises.target_answer: Die Liebe ist süß wie Honig, Ich habe Angst vor dem Arzt, Der Bauer hat Stolz, Der Pilot ist stolz, Der Ingenieur ist stolz auf das Haus, Der Gast ist sehr nett, Der Kellner ist wütend, Das Lied macht Freude, Der Held hat keine Angst, Die Gruppe tanzt mit Freude, Die Party macht Freude, die Freude am Reiten, Schach und Gitarre in der Freizeit
exercises.meaning: love, pride, anger, joy, fear — the five feelings
exercises.explanation: Five feelings, one frame. The frame never changes — sein + adjective — and the preposition carries the relationship: stolz auf, Angst vor, Freude mit. The old words feel them too: der Bauer hat Stolz, der Held hat keine Angst, der Kellner ist wütend.

exercises.prompt: Four feelings are native or ancient. One is a French loan that English also bought. Which?
exercises.meaning: nett ← French net ← Latin nitidus: the loan
exercises.explanation: die Liebe, wütend and stolz are native Germanic; die Freude is the froh family. nett is the new arrival: French net, 'clean', the same word English bought as neat — neat kept tidy, nett went warm.

exercises.prompt: 'die Liebe' is the same ancient root as its English twin — with the b where English writes v. Give the English twin:
exercises.explanation: love and Liebe are one root. The family also holds archaic English lief, 'dear', and the believe/glauben pair — the same root with the same prefix pattern, built on the root of love.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the evening sentence: 'We dance to the music'
exercises.explanation: zur = zu der, to the — music takes zu where English says to. And the pronoun is wir, the new one from the last lesson, doing its first feeling.
exercises.affirmation: Wir is we — the same word, one letter moved.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the schedule sentence: 'After school comes the sport'
exercises.target_answer: Nach der Schule kommt der Sport
exercises.explanation: nach + dative der Schule, and the verb comes second: Nach der Schule kommt der Sport. Time phrase first, verb second, subject third — the order German loves.

summary.outcome: Name the feelings — Liebe, nett, wütend, stolz, Freude — and attach them with auf, vor and mit.

use_example.german: Ich bin stolz auf das Haus — die Musik macht Freude.
use_example.english: I am proud of the house — the music brings joy.

summary.takeaway: die Liebe is love's twin with the b, nett is neat gone warm, die Freude is frolic's German home — and stolz has no twin: English bought French proud.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: five high-value adjectives — richtig, falsch, sauber, leer, offen — the last new words of the campaign.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Gefühle: die Liebe, nett, wütend, stolz, die Freude (After school comes the sport):
twist.target_answer: Nach der Schule kommt der Sport
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Nach der Schule kommt der Sport" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Gefühle: die Liebe, nett, wütend, stolz, die Freude without relying on short-term echo.

liebe.context_phrase: Die Liebe ist wichtig im Leben.
liebe.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *lubō — the explicit twin of English love; the noun of lieben. [wiktionary]

nett.etymology_derivation: From Old French net, Latin nitidus — Wiktionary: 'Compare English neat', a shared Romance loan. [wiktionary]

wütend.context_phrase: Er ist wütend auf seinen Bruder.
wütend.context_translation: He is angry at his brother.
wütend.etymology_derivation: wüten (to rage, the Wut family) + -end; no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

stolz.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stultaz 'proud, stiff' — English stout is the named cognate. [wiktionary]

freude.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *frawiþō, from the 'jump for joy' root; only Dutch cognates named — see Schadenfreude. [wiktionary]

arzt.context_translation: The doctor helps me a lot.
arzt.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German arzet, from Latin archīāter (chief healer); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

bauer.context_phrase: Der Bauer wohnt auf dem Hof.
bauer.context_translation: The farmer lives on the farm.
bauer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *būraz "dweller" — cognate with English boor, and with bower "dwelling". [wiktionary]

honig.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *hunag — Wiktionary: 'Cognate with English honey'. [wiktionary]

musik.etymology_derivation: From Latin mūsica — the same Latin loan as English music. [wiktionary]

sport.etymology_derivation: 19th-century borrowing from English sport — see treiben (to drive) in Ich treibe Sport. [wiktionary]

lied.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *leuþ 'song'; no modern English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

tanzen.etymology_derivation: From Old French dancer via Low German — the same French loan as English dance. [wiktionary]

pilot.etymology_derivation: Borrowed about 1500 from Italian pilota, partly via French pilote - the same Italian word that gave English pilot. [wiktionary][etymonline]

ingenieur.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French ingénieur — the same French loan as English engineer. [wiktionary]

wir.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *wīz — the very same pronoun as English we. [wiktionary]

schule.context_phrase: Die Schule beginnt um acht Uhr.
schule.etymology_derivation: From Latin (ultimately Greek scholē) — the same classical loan as English school; see Schüler. [wiktionary]

gast.context_phrase: Wir haben heute Gäste zum Essen.
gast.context_translation: We have guests for dinner today.
gast.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *gastiz, the exact twin of English guest; Latin hostis, enemy, shows the older guest-host pair. [wiktionary]

gruppe.context_phrase: Unsere Gruppe trifft sich um acht.
gruppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French groupe, from Italian gruppo, ultimately from Germanic *kruppaz, lump — the same Romance round-trip word as English group. [wiktionary]

held.etymology_derivation: From Proto-West Germanic *haliþ, hero, cognate with Old English hæleþ, a relative of the English health and hale family; the final th hardened to d. [wiktionary]

party.etymology_derivation: Unadapted borrowing from English party — a doublet of older loans Partei/Partie. [wiktionary]

gitarre.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from Spanish guitarra, from Arabic qithara, from Greek kithara - the same Spanish word that gave English guitar. [wiktionary]

reiten.context_translation: The child is learning to ride.
reiten.etymology_derivation: Class 1 strong verb from Proto-Germanic *rīdaną - the exact twin of English ride: reiten-ritt-geritten matches ride-rode-ridden. [wiktionary]

schach.etymology_derivation: From Arabic shah, from Persian shah (king) - the same word that gave English check and checkmate (Persian shah mat, the king is dead). [wiktionary][etymonline]

freizeit.context_phrase: In meiner Freizeit lese ich Bücher.
freizeit.context_translation: In my free time I read books.
freizeit.etymology_derivation: frei + Zeit, literally free time; frei is the exact twin of free and Zeit the twin of time (as in tide, t to z). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
